original: I heard the story of myself again last night, told across a crowded taproom by a man who had no notion he was telling it to the one it belonged to, and I have been turning it over ever since, the way you turn a stone you picked up without meaning to and now cannot quite bring yourself to set down.

snip: I did not know him, the man in the story. That is the plain truth of it, and plain truth is very nea
original: I did not know him, the man in the story. That is the plain truth of it, and plain truth is very near all I have left that is worth the giving. They had made me into someone in those tales: a figure, a wonder, a man who walked through the whole of his life already knowing the shape of it. In the tale he came up the valley already meaning the tower, saw the whole of it standing behind his eyes on the first morning, and raised it in a season, and the hill made no argument. He was never once wrong about a footing, never sat a winter counting silver, never stood in the rain arguing with a wagon. The tellers are fond of such men. And the man they made is, if I may say so of my own story, no one I ever met. Sure of himself. Untouched by anything. Always the right word ready on his lips and never a wrong night lying behind him. I would not cross a room to shake his hand, and I have yet to hear the tale told in a way that made me wish I would.

original: I had never meant to stay in it long, for that matter. Coming home to my father's house was to be a stopgap, a place to keep myself and my boots while my own house went up across the river; and my own was to be a wonder, or a warning, depending on which of us you asked about it afterward: grander than anything my father would have put his name to, taller, flashier, altogether more foolish, the same clean lines he had given my mother swollen to twice the scale and three times the cost, a great bright thing built to stand as a gift and a grand gesture ahead of a wedding. I had drawn a good part of it myself, in the good years, when I still supposed I knew what I was building toward. There was no wedding, in the end, and so no need of the house. I never lived in it. For three years it had stood across the water full of a life that had not happened, costing me a small fortune a year in the bare keeping of a grand thing that nobody used, and I could no more sell it than cross its threshold. Penworth had spent the better part of that winter trying, with a delicacy that cost him something to keep up, to talk me round to letting it go, for the sake of my purse and, though he was too careful a man to say it, for the sake of the rest of me; and I had spent the winter not answering him.

snip: The first and easier part of it I had come by rail: three days out of Vethmark in a carriage that ra
original: The first and easier part of it I had come by rail: three days out of Vethmark in a carriage that rattled the teeth in a man's head and let the cold in at every seam. The railways were new then, and it showed. The engine that hauled us was a crude, soot-breathing thing, all iron and steam and appetite, and there was next to nothing of the arcane in it, which surprised the sort of people who supposed a wizard must approve of a train on principle. I did not, particularly. You may put a working into a machine, and I have put a good many into a good many; but a working has to be fed and tended and coaxed and renewed, and one big enough to shoulder a train up a grade would have eaten more in the keeping than the coal it saved. That is the arithmetic people get backwards about my trade. There is no shortage of magic in this world; there has never been a shortage of magic. What the world is short of is people who can work it. The talent is born, not made. The Conclave sharpens it where it appears, and it appears seldom, and more seldom than it once did. Coal the world has by the mountain, iron by the shire, stokers by the thousand for the hiring; of those born able to set a lasting working into iron it has a scattered handful, every one of them wanted in six places at once. Put the whole of that little company to nursing locomotives and you might keep one railway arcane, and nothing else in the world would ever be warded or mended or lit again. So no sane man spends a wizard where a stoker will serve, and the railways ran on fire and water and brute iron cleverness and almost no magic at all, and I spent a fair part of those three days watching the engine hiss and labor at the watering-stops and thinking, in the idle, itching way of a man who cannot let a made thing alone, how much smaller and quieter and cleverer the whole of it could have been built, if the world had only had the hands to spare for it. It did not. It never has. That is the first hard fact of my trade, and the trains were a great smoking monument to it: a mountain of crude iron doing loudly and dearly what a very little good artifice could have done well, had there only been enough good artifice to go around, which there was not, and is not, and I have stopped expecting there ever to be.

snip: The inn stood where the street widened toward the beck. It was a broad, comfortable-looking building
original: The inn stood where the street widened toward the beck. It was a broad, comfortable-looking building of three storeys, one of the few in Ardenmoor to stand so tall, with a painted sign gone too weathered to read and lamplight already spilling out of its windows into the blue evening. I have stopped at a great many inns and could write a dull and honest book on the subject. This one, before I had so much as got down off my horse, had the one quality that matters and cannot be built on purpose: it looked like somewhere a tired man might stop being tired for a while. I got down, and my legs told me at length exactly how far we had come. A boy came out of the inn-yard shadows to take Snow's head with the unhurried competence of a child who has been around horses since before he could walk.

original: Cael came in on the tail of the meal, the cold of the evening still on his shoulders and his grandson at his heel. He was not the man I had built out of Penworth's correspondence; I had made him older and grander in my head. He was a solid man on the near side of old, not young but a fair way yet from grey, in a good plain coat, with a face that had done a great deal of weather in its time and a pair of eyes that had lost none of their sharpness to it. He looked me over the way you look at a thing you have been expecting for months and are pleased, on the whole, to find is real. His glance caught a moment on my face, as people's often did, and came up a good way short of my true count of years. I was past forty by then, and have never worn it where a man can see. Whatever figure he settled on he kept to himself, which I liked him for.

snip: There was no thread of fate in it, whatever a story would want. I did not come to Ardenmoor drawn by
original: There was no thread of fate in it, whatever a story would want. I did not come to Ardenmoor drawn by anything grander than an errand. I came because Penworth had an unerring eye and I had learned to trust it over my own; because it was spring, and I had spent the whole of the winter shut up in a quiet Vethmark townhouse with the spare rooms closed and sheeted, keeping well out of the way of the noise and the standing crowd of small obligations that a city presses on a man whether he asks for them or not, and had barely marked the season going by; and because there was nowhere else in the wide world I would rather have been, which in those days was less a boast than a fairly bleak measure of how small my life had got. *A hill of no agricultural worth and considerable quiet.* When I read that, it sounded like very nearly the only thing left that I wanted.

snip: We walked the whole of it, that afternoon, the long slow way round, the way you walk a thing you mea
original: We walked the whole of it, that afternoon, the long slow way round, the way you walk a thing you mean to be answerable for. Cael went at the pace his knees allowed and I was glad of it, because it was the right pace for the ground, slow enough to see. He showed me the spring that came up cold and clear out of the hill's south face and had never once, in living memory or his grandmother's, gone dry; a thing worth more than the hill on top of it, he said, and he was right, and I would have cause to bless that spring a hundred times in the years after. He showed me the woodland strip, good mixed timber, oak and ash and a stand of larch a former owner had planted and not lived to cut. He showed me where the grade eased along the eastern slope into a shelf of deeper, greener grass, and I felt something about that shelf that I had not the knowledge yet to name and did not mention, and Cael did not mention it either, though I caught him watching me not mention it. And all the while the boy Soren went ahead of us and to the side, quiet as weather, stopping now and then to crouch over some particular patch of ground with the total absorption of a child at his real work, and once, near the crown, he stood for a long moment with his bare hand flat on a stone, and then took it off, and came on, and said nothing, and I thought nothing of it, which is a thing I would give a good deal to go back and un-think.

snip: And there is this, besides. Once in a great while, in some inn a long way from anywhere, I will hear
original: And there is this, besides. Once in a great while, in some inn a long way from anywhere, I will hear a story told that I half recognize, the way you might recognize your own coat on a stranger three sizes too large for it. There are not many of them. I am not, whatever you may have been led to expect, a man they sing about; I took a good deal of quiet care, over the years, that it should stay so. But a few tales got loose all the same, and time and retelling have warped them so far out of true that the man in them is half myth and half plain nonsense, and I would not know him to nod to in the road, and, if I am honest, do not much care for him. I hold the tellers no grudge; a good story is a kind of coin, and it is meant to be spent. It only seems a poor thing to leave nothing behind but those few, and so, if only so that the truth of it should exist somewhere, in one place, I mean to set down what actually happened. Or near enough. I will not pretend the years have warmed no words nor softened any faces; fondness does that, and I was fond of very nearly all of them, and they are gone now, every one of them, but me. Still, the shape of it is true, and the shape is the thing that matters.

snip: I rode down into the village at a walk, and it looked me over the way a small village looks over a s
original: I rode down into the village at a walk, and it looked me over the way a small village looks over a stranger, not unkindly but thoroughly, and then mostly went back to its evening. A hammer was still going somewhere among the houses, a smith at work past his hour, the ring of it carrying flat and clear across the cold. Further on, a shop breathed out the smell of an herbalist's trade as I passed its door, cut green stems and something bitter-clean beneath them, the smell of a place people go to when they are frightened for someone they love. Then it was behind me, and there was lamplight, and woodsmoke, and the good ordinary sound of a day being put away.

snip: Inside, the inn was warm and low-beamed and half full of the evening's regulars, and the woman behin
original: Inside, the inn was warm and low-beamed and half full of the evening's regulars, and the woman behind the bar took one look at me and had the whole of it before I had crossed the room, the road and the errand and the name. Her name was Lira. She kept that inn the way a good captain keeps a ship, which is to say invisibly and completely, and she had been expecting me the better part of a week. She was a spare, measured woman who gave a stranger nothing he had not paid for, neither warmth nor its opposite, and it was a good while before I understood that this was not coldness in her but economy. She kept her regard the way she kept her good glasses, and did not bring it out for just anyone.

snip: "Aye, that sounds like him." Cael took a cup from Lira with a nod that had a long friendship folded
original: "Aye, that sounds like him." Cael took a cup from Lira with a nod that had a long friendship folded up inside it. "Well. He'll have told you the shape of it. The hill, and the land about it, and the price. The price is fair, and it's settled, and the most of it was never mine to haggle anyway. What your man has been buying up is half a dozen holdings: dead men's fields, parish ground, other families' tired acres. I speak for the lot of them tonight because somebody had to and I've been here longest. So we'll not be bargaining, you and I. That part's done." He looked at me over the top of the cup. "I'll tell you what's not done. A stranger nobody in this valley can put a name to comes up the road from who knows where and buys the better part of its idle ground in one hand. That sits ill with folk, and it ought to. So the families sent the oldest man they had to come and look at you, and here I am, looking." He said it without heat, the way a man reports weather. "The fields I'll say no more about. They want working, and they'll be glad of any man who means to work them. The hill's the one piece of it I'd have kept back. The hill was ours, my family's, and I've had money in my hand for it before now, slate men and tin men, coin as good as yours, and I sent every one of them back down the road. A hill is not a purse you turn out and pocket. It is a thing a man stands on, and does something with, and answers for. If I sell it, I sell it to someone who means to make something of it, not to a man who means only to carry it off in carts." He turned his cup a slow quarter-turn on the table and did not drink from it. "My grandmother loved that rise of ground past all sense. Past all sense. She'd go up it in every weather to the year she died." He tipped his head toward the boy, who was studying the fire and missing nothing. "I was younger than that one there when she swore it to me. She swore that on the right kind of still evening, if you sat quiet on the top of it, you could hear it."

snip: "Then here's what I'd say," he went on, brisker now, as if the matter were settled in him and only t
original: "Then here's what I'd say," he went on, brisker now, as if the matter were settled in him and only the arrangements were left. "It's full dark, and nothing worth buying ever looks like much at dusk. Take your room. Sleep. Walk up in the morning, when there's light to show you the truth of the place, and stand on it a while before you decide anything. If you still want it by noon, we'll go find Penworth's man and make an honest tangle of paperwork out of it, and I'll have sold my grandmother's hill to someone she'd have approved of, which is the most I've hoped for out of this business from the start." He got to his feet again by the same slow arrangement. "A man ought to look at a hill before he owns it. That's all the wisdom I've got, but I'm fairly sure of it."

I woke before I meant to and lay a while listening to the village wake around me, the beck, the first cart, a rooster with strong feelings and no sense of pitch, and then I went down, and Lira set porridge and honey and a slab of bacon in front of me and left me to eat it in peace.

snip: I will not pretend to you that anything happened up there. The honest truth is that I climbed a hill
original: I will not pretend to you that anything happened up there. The honest truth is that I climbed a hill and stood on the top of it and was not, that morning, visited by anything at all: no revelation, no lifting of the heart, none of the things a man is supposed to feel on a hilltop. I had not rightly known what I expected, and so was neither let down by the want of it nor carried away by anything in its place. What the crown gave me was a view and a great sweeping quiet, and both were worth the walk. The whole valley lay open below me, Ardenmoor small and smoking at the bottom of it, the beck a bright wandering thread, the fields laid out in their first green, new-made and not yet finished. If there was anything at all uncommon in the place, it was only the quiet itself, which lay over the crown a little deeper than the height alone quite accounted for; but a tired man with a long road behind him can talk himself into and out of a great many things before breakfast, and I let the view have me instead. To the north the land folded into dark woodland, and out of the middle of that wood one great old oak stood up alone above the rest, bare-crowned and black against the morning, keeping its own counsel. I did not know then what that tree was to the hill I stood on, nor that the two of them had been holding a conversation between them for longer than there had been a village below to name it. I only marked it, the way you mark a thing that stands apart, and thought it a fine old tree, and turned back to the valley.

original: The elder of the two I marked before I knew his trade, the way you sometimes do, because he had the particular stillness of a man who is good with his hands and has never once needed to say so. He was broad and grey and unhurried, and he ate without waste and without any part of him left over. When he set his cup down he set it down square to the edge of the table, and then squared it a second time with one finger though it had not needed it. That afternoon he was only a big grey man eating his dinner, and I was only the stranger the whole room was pretending with great courtesy not to watch.

snip: We had come up by then onto the first of the rough, where the walls give out and the wind owns the g
original: We had come up by then onto the first of the rough, where the walls give out and the wind owns the grass, and he swung his stick at the whole grey shoulder of it. "And the high ground, all of it, the fell and the scrub above the tree line that runs back off the top of your hill farther than you'll walk in a day, that was nobody's and everybody's, sheep-run and weather; good ground enough in its way, and never once asked to be anything, for there's no man round here these forty years has had the money to ask it. Your man had the parish and the township set their marks to the whole of it, so it's yours now on the map, every stone and grouse of it. You've more land than the squire down at Wainford, on the paper. You've not four hundred acres of it a plough has been over in ten years. Both of those are true, and you'd best learn to carry them in the one hand, for the valley will." He stopped on the path and turned and looked at me, and there was nothing unkind in it. "Land wants two things, and it's the same two things everywhere I've ever heard of. It wants hands and it wants a road. You've bought yourself a deal of land with neither, and I'd not have you find that out in your own time and think we'd hidden it. A stake in the mill-pond water besides. That agent of his sat at my table three evenings running with a map and a pencil, and every evening the map got bigger and the pencil got sharper. I've sold land my whole life. I never once sold it to a man who wanted the ground his ground would need before his ground needed it, nor took the trouble to square the bits nobody else had ever thought worth the bother."

snip: He turned and looked at me then, straight, an old man laying the truth on the table between us where
original: He turned and looked at me then, straight, an old man laying the truth on the table between us where I could not miss it. "So there it is, and you'll have it from me and not from the tavern. That's what you're buying. A hill that put my father on his knees and has thrown off every roof and wall any soul has tried to set on it in the two lifetimes I can account for. My grandmother loved it and heard God-knows-what in it and left it to me and I've kept it forty years for no reason I could ever say aloud, and now here's you, come up a bad road with a wizard's trade and a dead man's..." He stopped himself, gently, on whatever he had seen in my face when he was not looking, and did not finish it, and went on more quietly. "And quiet you're after, right enough. I'll not cheat you, is my whole point. If you buy this hill you may spend a great many years and a great deal of your man's money learning what my father learned in one summer. I'd think less of myself if I let you sign without hearing it said."

snip: I have been offered a great many bargains in my time, and flattered and hurried and lied to over mos
original: I have been offered a great many bargains in my time, and flattered and hurried and lied to over most of them, and none of them ever moved me to close a deal so fast as that old man doing his level best to talk me out of one. But it was not only the honesty, though the honesty was a great part of it. It was that he had told me the hill threw off everything set upon it, and I had stood on the crown of it that morning and felt, for the first time in three years, the wanting of a thing take hold of *me*; and I was arrogant enough, or wounded enough, or simply wizard enough, to wonder whether the two facts might be the same fact wearing two faces. His father had asked the hill for a level floor and four square walls, had *told* it, the way a fair and stubborn mason tells any ground what it will do. I did not yet have the words for what I suspected, but I had the shape of it already, standing there in the gold light, and the shape of it was this: that there is a great difference between a thing that cannot be built on, and a thing that has never once been *asked*.

snip: That night I sat up late at the little table under the eaves at Lira's, with a borrowed candle and m
original: That night I sat up late at the little table under the eaves at Lira's, with a borrowed candle and my own traveling ink, and wrote to Penworth. It was not a long letter; Penworth did not reward long letters, only precise ones. I told him I had seen the hill and walked the bounds and shaken on the whole of it with the seller, at his figure, and that he was to finish it, all of it, the purchase and the parcels and the water rights, and to spare no care over the water rights in particular, as I had seen the spring and would build my life around it. I told him the seller was an honest man named Cael and was to be dealt with as such. I did not tell him that I meant to build on ground that had never let itself be built on, nor that the wanting of it had taken hold of me, nor any of the rest of it; Penworth would learn what he needed as he needed it, and worry over exactly the right amount, which in Penworth was a great deal. I signed it, and sealed it, and set it by for the morning post, and then I put out the candle and sat a while in the dark with the small window open a crack to the cold.

snip: The second reason was the first one wearing a different coat. Scarcely an acre of that ground had ev
original: The second reason was the first one wearing a different coat. Scarcely an acre of that ground had ever been put in the way of earning anything. I had assumed, in my ignorance, that cheap land meant bad land, and Penworth had the goodness to correct me in writing before I could embarrass myself with it aloud. Ground is not worth what it will grow, he wrote. Ground is worth what it can carry to a market, and every mile between the two comes off the price. The soil in those bottoms was as good as any I have stood on since. There was water everywhere, and timber on the slopes, and grazing on the high ground enough to keep a valley in wool. And it was worth next to nothing, because there was no road out worth the name, not a drain cut nor a fence standing over the most of it, no barns, no byres, and hardly a soul within a day's walk who was free to work it. A man who buys such a place is not buying a farm. He is buying the makings of one, and the making is all still in front of him, and it is the making and not the buying that costs.

snip: Cheap, and it still took very nearly every silver I could put a hand to. That is a different thing a
original: Cheap, and it still took very nearly every silver I could put a hand to. That is a different thing altogether from everything I had, as I have learned since. Penworth spent the winter turning my affairs over in his careful hands to see what they would bear, and what they bore was a great deal on paper and almost nothing in coin. The river house was the most of my worth, and the river house would not move quickly; a grand house in a great city is a slow animal, and that one stood on ground I had never owned and carried a debt I had signed for in a better year, so that when it went at last it would come to me halved. Rather than sit and wait on it, Penworth borrowed against it: a short loan out of a bank that knew the street the house stood in and cared nothing whatever for the country I was going to, the whole of it to fall due when the sale cleared, and a sale of that size clears at the pace of its lawyers, which Penworth priced, as he priced everything, at very nearly a year. Set beside that were the old patents, which paid their steady quarterly pittance whether I attended to them or not, and my father's firm, which went on paying its small partner's share into an account I never opened. My father's house did not appear in the columns at all. Penworth knew better than to put it there, and I would not have signed the page it was on. He ruled it out for me in a letter, in neat columns, and at the foot of the columns stood a sum aimed like a spent arrow at a hill nobody wanted, and the loosing of it left me holding five thousand acres and next to no money, a condition I had no name for then and have never since been entirely out of. That was the mercy in the thing, and the whole of the trap. So nothing at all fell due until the place had been given a full turn of the seasons to find its feet, which was not generosity but conveyancing, and it meant that in a year I would need this hill to be earning, one way or another, or the note would begin, quietly and then not quietly, to eat me. The farmland in the bottoms would have to be got into the hands of tenants who would work it and pay for the working. The trade would have to come. A wiser man would have looked at that year the way you look at a lit fuse, and been frightened. I looked at it and felt, for the first time in three years, interested. I have learned to trust that in myself further than I trust my caution, though it has cost me nearly as often as it has paid.

snip: A village the size of Ardenmoor does not decide about a man quickly, and is right not to. For the fi
original: A village the size of Ardenmoor does not decide about a man quickly, and is right not to. For the first of those weeks I was served at Lira's promptly and correctly and with about the warmth of a signed receipt, which suited me well, for it asked nothing of me in return. I was the wizard who had bought Cael's hill, and that is a thing to be watched a while before it is a thing to be welcomed. So I did not hurry it. I paid what I owed on the day I owed it, and said good morning to men who did not yet say it back, and kept my strangeness folded up small and out of sight, and let the place look at me as long as it cared to. Once, early, one of the quarrymen leaned over from the next bench, emboldened by his cups, and asked me straight out whether it was true I was a wizard, and what that meant a man could do. I told him it meant mostly that I could ruin an evening explaining what it did not mean, and I bought him a drink, and he went away satisfied. After that I was, if not a friend, then at least a known quantity, which in a village is the first step toward the rest.

snip: The wagons came up on a grey soft afternoon with rain not far off, groaning and lurching along the l
original: The wagons came up on a grey soft afternoon with rain not far off, groaning and lurching along the last of the giving-up road with the drivers walking at the horses' heads over the worst of it. I went down to meet them at the foot of the hill, and Soren came from wherever he kept himself and fell in beside me without being asked, and the two of us and the two drivers spent a wet and satisfying couple of hours carrying my life up the track by hand where the wagons could not go. There is a plain honesty to carrying a thing up a hill. The boy worked without being told and without complaint, and had a good eye for how a load wants to sit, and I marked it and said nothing, for I had already learned that saying a thing to that boy was the surest way to make him careful of it.

snip: There is a particular pleasure, and a particular grief, in unpacking the tools of a trade in a new p
original: There is a particular pleasure, and a particular grief, in unpacking the tools of a trade in a new place. The books had come up in crates I had packed myself and trusted to no one else, the better part of a lifetime's reading and a fair share of its writing, and I stacked them under the oilcloth in no order at all and knew already the long good evenings I would spend giving them one. My instruments I was more careful of. They are fewer than folk imagine and stranger, the fine-drawn things a man in my line uses to feel for what is already in a place before ever he asks it for anything: gauges and glasses and lengths of drawn wire that mean nothing to the eye and a great deal to the hand, each wrapped in its own cloth against the jolting of the road. I laid them out under cover and ran my hands over them in the failing light, taking their count, and it came to me that I had not opened most of these cases in three years, and that I had packed them, when I packed them, the way you pack the effects of the dead, without any real expectation of wanting them again. Now here they were on a wet hill, wanting to be wanted. It is a strange thing to be outlived by your own tools.

snip: It was not large; a strong man could have carried it, though the drivers had chosen not to, and I di
original: It was not large; a strong man could have carried it, though the drivers had chosen not to, and I did not blame them, for there are things the body declines to shoulder alone before the mind has troubled to say why. It was old, older than anything else I owned, black wood banded in a metal that was not iron and had never rusted. It had no keyhole any locksmith would know and no lock any key would turn, because the lock on it was mine and was not the kind you open with your hands. I had made that binding myself, years before, in another life, and had not unmade it since, and did not mean to. What was inside it was mine and no one else's. I had carried it out of the wreck of everything and into that dark sheeted house, and now up this wet hill, and I handled it always with more care than I handled anything I owned, myself in those years included.

And I stood in the last grey wet of the evening on the crown of my own hill with everything I owned in the world stacked in oilcloth behind me, and found that I did not, after all, want to go down to the inn.
revised: The drivers took their wagons away before the light was wholly gone, glad, I think, to be quit of the tiny village and the rain and the chest, and Soren went off down the track to his grandfather's fire. snip: So I made a camp. I had a good tent of waxed canvas that had kept the weather off me across country
original: So I made a camp. I had a good tent of waxed canvas that had kept the weather off me across country a man could not cross in a year, and I pitched it near the crown in the lee of the one shoulder of ground that offered any. I dug a fire-pit and coaxed a fire out of the dry heart of wood the rain had not yet reached, and set my kettle in the coals and made tea in the smell of woodsmoke and wet grass and canvas, which is one of the oldest and kindest smells there is. The chest I brought inside the tent and set at my back and did not look at. I ate bread and cheese carried up from Lira's, and sat in the door of my tent with the fire dying and the valley below me putting out its lamps one window at a time, and was as nearly at peace as I had been since a letter came three weeks late in another spring.

original: I lodged at Lira's while the paper went back and forth, and for a good while after. I had thought, when I took the room, that I would want it a night or two and no more; I kept it the better part of the season, mostly empty, a bolt-hole I paid for by the week and slept in by the fortnight, and if Lira thought anything of a man paying for a bed he was not in, she kept it in the ledger with everything else she was not saying. Lira let me the room by the week without comment, and fed me without comment, and formed her opinion of me the way she formed all her opinions, slowly and to herself, and let it out a word at a time over the weeks, the way you let out a coat you mean to keep.

snip: I have said I meant to learn the hill before I asked anything of it, and for the first weeks of that
original: I have said I meant to learn the hill before I asked anything of it, and for the first weeks of that summer I did nothing else. It is not a thing you can hurry, and it is not, to a man watching from the lane below, a thing that looks like work at all. I walked the ground in the early part of the day and the late. I lay on it at the hours it chose to speak and let the two slow pulses come up into me, the one at the failing of the light and the one in the cold before the birds, until I could have told you when they were coming the way you can tell a familiar step on a stair. I set out the instruments of my trade on a folding table under the canvas, the gauges and the glasses and the lengths of drawn wire, and I used them the way I had been taught to use them, which is to say to listen with, and not to command. A man in my line spends the better half of his life learning that the second thing is a good way to get himself killed, and the other half forgetting it.

original: Not that the real one was any great prize. I will not sit here in my old age and pretend the man I was in those days was wiser or gentler or one whit less of a fool than the figure in the story. God knows I had a great deal more to learn than I yet had the sense to know I was missing, and I learned the most of it the slow way, and late, and at a cost to better people than myself. But he was a man, at least, and not a monument. And if I am to leave one true thing behind me when I go, I would sooner it were him than the bright bronze figure the years have cast up in his place.

original: Perhaps I will set the true thing down one day. The wanting to has come over me lately, quiet and from behind, the way most of my worse ideas have arrived. And when I turn my mind to how it would have to go, I find I know at least where it would not begin. Not on a wonder, and not on a boy. There is no boy in it, whatever the tellers would prefer, and no wonder either, not at the start of it. I think I would begin with the man himself, such as he was in those days: at the tired end of a bad few years, with far more skill than he had sense and nowhere in all the wide world that he needed to be. And I think, before I let him take a single step, I would ask you to go easy on him. He did not yet know how any of it would turn out.

snip: Penworth was my man of affairs, and the running of my whole tangled life had been his for something
original: Penworth was my man of affairs, and the running of my whole tangled life had been his for something over a decade by then. He kept the letters, the monies, and the small steady mountain of paper any working life throws off whether a man attends to it or not. He was a spare, precise, exceedingly formal gentleman out of Vethmark, near enough my own age and a good deal tidier about the wearing of it, and he had a particular genius, earned across a long career spent in the disorder of other men's affairs, for finding me things before I knew I wanted them, and for quietly buying the ground under a thing while I was still making up my mind about the thing itself. His letter had reached me at the turn of the year, and I had carried it about ever since, folded twice and gone soft at the creases from a season in my coat. It was a small marvel of its kind: three close pages to tell me he had come across a piece of country he believed would suit me, *a hill of no agricultural worth and considerable quiet*; that he had taken the liberty of securing it provisionally, along with a good breadth of the workable land about it, the sort you could set to honest tenants and thereafter forget you owned; and that he would count it a personal kindness if I would go and look at what I had nearly purchased before he made me finish the purchasing.

snip: The townhouse I had wintered in was my father's before it was mine, and my father had been an archit
original: The townhouse I had wintered in was my father's before it was mine, and my father had been an architect, which is to say a man who drew the houses that other men then lived their whole lives inside of. He had built up a small firm about the doing of it, a good and unglamorous one that outlived him and stands drawing houses yet, and I hold his share in it still, though I have not troubled it in years and it has had the grace not to trouble me. I had learned the drawing at his elbow as a boy, and paid my own way through my schooling with drafting work at a board of my own, before I ever took up any stranger trade.

He had built up a small firm about the doing of it, a respected one that outlived him and stands yet, and I hold his share in it still. I had learned drawing at his elbow as a boy, and paid my own way through my schooling with drafting work at a board of my own, before I ever took up any stranger trade.

snip: The house he kept for himself he had drawn years before, for my mother, early, when the firm was sti
original: The house he kept for himself he had drawn years before, for my mother, early, when the firm was still more hope than trade and he built as much for the love of the thing as for the money in it. It was the finest small thing he ever set his hand to, and it stood in what had then been a quiet, unfashionable quarter of the city, the sort of street a young man of modest means could still afford a corner of. The quarter had not stayed unfashionable. The town had grown up around it in the years since, gone dear and grand, tall bright houses rising to either side until my father's modest little place sat among them like an honest word in an ornate sentence, worth many times over what it had cost him to raise and not a coin of that worth for anything he would have troubled to count. When the two of them were gone it came to me, and I had grown up in those rooms and been happy in them, in the years when the house smelled of drawing-ink and my mother's baking and the windows stood open on the garden half the year, and I came back to them, after everything, the way a man goes back to the one place that never once asked him to be anything more than he was.

snip: The line gave out, as such lines do, exactly where the paying traffic did, at a raw and cheerful tow
original: The line gave out, as such lines do, exactly where the paying traffic did, at a raw and cheerful town called Wainford that lived to pour the country's grain and cattle into railway cars and held no higher opinion of itself. There the rails simply stopped, and the country they had never troubled to reach began. I got Snow down out of the horse-box, the two of us equally glad to be quit of the noise, and from there we went on the old way, by horse and by road, four more days into the green silence.

I got Snow down out of the horse-box, the two of us equally glad to be quit of the noise, and from there we went on the old way, by horse and by road, four more days into the green silence.

snip: There was a hill to the north of the village and a little east of it, rounded and green and crowned
original: There was a hill to the north of the village and a little east of it, rounded and green and crowned with nothing but weather. I marked it the way you mark any rise of ground you have ridden a long way to look at. *That will be the one*, I thought, and thought no more of it than that. It was a hill. I had seen a thousand hills. Whatever it had to say for itself, it was keeping to itself, and I was glad enough of the quiet.
